props.title: Attack
props.initialSlug: WWII captain faces betrayal in brutal combat drama

sections.content: **Attack** (1956) stands as one of the most brutal and unflinching anti-war films of the 1950s. Director Robert Aldrich, fresh off his noir success with **Kiss Me Deadly** (1955), brings that same raw intensity to this World War II drama. The film follows Lt. Costa (Jack Palance) as he confronts the cowardice of his commanding officer, Captain Cooney (Eddie Albert), whose failures have already caused unnecessary deaths. Unlike the patriotic war films of the era like **To Hell and Back** (1955), Aldrich's film dares to explore military corruption, failed leadership, and the psychological toll of combat.

sections.content: The film's influence rippled through war cinema, paving the way for more critical examinations of military leadership like Paths of Glory (1957) and later **Platoon** (1986). Palance delivers a powerhouse performance that strips away Hollywood's glamorization of combat. The claustrophobic tank sequences and tense confrontations in cramped command posts create an atmosphere of mounting dread that influenced later films like **Lebanon** (2009) and **Fury** (2014).

What sets **Attack** apart is its unflinching portrayal of moral corruption within the military chain of command. While films like **The Bridge on the River Kwai** (1957) explored similar themes through metaphor and allegory, Aldrich confronts these issues head-on. The film's controversial ending, where justice comes through violence rather than military protocol, challenged the Production Code restrictions of the time and influenced later anti-war films like The Hill (1965) and **Casualties of War** (1989). sections.content: **Attack** revolutionized how Hollywood depicted military leadership, creating a template for showing flawed commanders that influenced films from **Breaker Morant** (1980) to **Saving Private Ryan** (1998). The film's exploration of battlefield ethics and the limits of obedience to authority resonated deeply during the Cold War era, particularly in films like **Dr. Strangelove** (1964) and **The Bedford Incident** (1965).
